extracted.intended_audience: Public Information Officers (PIOs) and communications staff in public safety / emergency management
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for Public Information Officers on creating written public information products (news releases, statements, talking points, web/social content) and performing media relations during emergencies and steady-state operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that make an incident or activity appropriate for a news release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timeliness, proximity, conflict, impact, prominence, uniqueness, and human interest when deciding to issue a news release. Use a news release when an activity/incident is newsworthy and a statement will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: News release content standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Core content and writing standards for a news release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate, factual information; use clear, concise, easy-to-understand language; write simple sentences and short paragraphs; write in third person; attribute facts; avoid jargon and acronyms. Organize facts with a strong lead that answers Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How; present most important facts first, then supporting facts, less important facts, background information, and social media add-ons.

rubrics_metrics.name: News release format and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended physical and stylistic format for news releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Associated Press (AP) style. Normally one page, single spaced, on organization letterhead. Include contact information, date (time optional), news release number, and continuation/end markers such as 'More' and 'End' or '# # #' or -30-.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the right written product
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the written product type to match purpose, audience, and content complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match product to purpose (answer a question, inform/announce, educate, clarify, ask for action), target audience needs, and subject complexity. Options include statements, fact sheets, media advisories, PSAs, newsletter articles, brochures/fliers, talking points, and news releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-driven product selection
rubrics_metrics.description: How purpose influences choice of product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a statement when less detail is needed than in a news release. Use a fact sheet for more detail. Use a media advisory to invite media to events; PSAs to enlist electronic media cooperation; brochures/fliers to supplement releases without overwhelming reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key message development
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and use a clear key message to guide communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your key message is the #1 thing you want the audience to know or do. Use it to target audience, anticipate questions, develop supporting information (facts, instructions, comparisons), select appropriate medium, and ensure consistent communication across partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting information and talking points
rubrics_metrics.description: Use supporting facts and talking points to validate and convey key messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting information validates key messages and addresses audience concerns. Talking points are brief, spoken statements (1–2 sentences) written for the ear, memorable and quotable; intended for internal use during interviews and product development. Consider three bullets per key message: past, present, future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon and acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity requirement to ensure public comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid internal jargon and acronyms in public-facing products; they can be barriers to communicating with the public. If acronyms must be used, define them for public audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AP style and journalist-friendly conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conform to journalist expectations to increase pick-up and usability of materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow The Associated Press Stylebook. Structure releases in the inverted pyramid where appropriate, provide clear contact info, and supply usable, reporter-friendly material (ready quotes, facts, background).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing for the Web and social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust writing approach for online and social platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the most important information first (inverted pyramid), use clear and concise language, short sentences and paragraphs, chunk content, use visuals/multimedia, use audience words to optimize search, and consider platform character limits. Repurpose content for social platforms but avoid verbatim reuse. Follow organizational clearance/social media policy and measure success with metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media tone and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: How to write and structure social media posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a conversational tone (contractions, pronouns), put intriguing info upfront, use fewer characters than allowed, reuse content thoughtfully, use tagging/mentions to link partners, and stay current with platform features and analytics. Know your organization's clearance policy for social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: PIO core qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal and professional qualities that contribute to PIO effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be analytical, strategic, proactive, knowledgeable, assertive, credible/trusted, flexible, able to perform under pressure, and accessible. Accessibility to media is especially crucial; credibility is built by returning calls and delivering what you promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media relations skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices to build credibility and productive media relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide information and access to newsmakers, demonstrate understanding of media needs and operations, respect media deadlines, maintain open dialogue, and consider regular meetings or briefings with media. Develop a policy on working with the media and engage media in steady-state relationship-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Information System (JIS) / JIC functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Roles and expected activities of JIS/Pio and the Joint Information Center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JIS integrates information and public affairs across command structures to deliver consistent, coordinated, accurate, accessible, timely, and complete information. PIO functions include advising command, gathering/verifying/coordinating/disseminating information, handling inquiries, providing warnings, and rumor monitoring. A JIC is the central location for JIS operations; normally a single JIC but flexible to multiple if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident information cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Four-step operational cycle for managing incident information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather complete information; verify information for accuracy; coordinate with other public information personnel to ensure consistency; disseminate consistent, coordinated, accurate, accessible, timely, and complete information to the public and stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go Kit and preparedness resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential tools and pre-arranged services needed for PIO operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a Go Kit (office supplies, laptop/tablet/smartphone, portable printer/alternate power, maps, recording equipment, extra batteries, camera, radio, agency letterhead, pre-scripted messages, template releases). Establish agreements/contracts with translation services, printers, and communications providers (WiFi/cell) before incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing for media interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps to prepare for an interview or spokesperson appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the best spokesperson, develop objectives, consider the audience, develop key messages and materials, obtain clearance/approval, and practice/prep the spokesperson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview DOs
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended behaviors during media interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know what you want to say and use talking points; stick to your main point; be positive yet realistic; turn negatives into positives; show compassion and empathy; stop when you've made your point; avoid speculation; summarize key points at the end when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview DON'Ts
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviors to avoid during media interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't speculate or answer hypotheticals, don't comment on matters best answered by other agencies, don't repeat unverified statements from others, never lose your temper, never lie, never say anything you don't want printed, and avoid saying 'No comment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to 'No comment'
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases to use instead of 'No comment' to remain transparent yet appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use alternatives such as: 'The matter is under investigation and that information is not available at this time.'; 'We will provide updates as more information becomes available.'; 'Let me put you in contact with someone who is better able to answer that question.'; 'Those details are covered by the Privacy Act and I cannot discuss them, but I can give you this general information...'. Use responses suited to the situation and be careful not to promise updates unless you will provide them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging / transitional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases to steer an interview back to your key messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bridges like: 'What is most important is...'; 'What we should focus on is...'; 'What the public should know is...'; 'The point is...'; 'I don’t know, but what I can tell you is…' to redirect focus to your messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonverbal communication and appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on body language, voice, and attire during interviews and public appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain eye contact with the reporter (not the camera), speak clearly and modulate voice, appear attentive and sincere, align body with interviewer, use natural but controlled gestures, avoid distracting movement, dress conservatively and appropriately for the audience/channel, avoid bright whites/stripes/complicated patterns, remove sunglasses/hat and distracting jewelry; consider HD broadcast color issues and agency policies on badges/tattoos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing nervousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques to reduce interview anxiety and improve performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and practice talking points, anticipate reporter questions, use relaxation techniques (deep breaths, stretch), channel nervousness as positive energy, pause to gather thoughts instead of using filler words, and ask to try again if taped.

rubrics_metrics.name: What all news media need
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential accommodations and behaviors to support media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide prompt answers, access to the scene and to policymakers/responders, fair treatment, respect for deadlines, and rapid updates/corrections as incidents evolve. Understand and comply with freedom of information/sunshine laws to the extent required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media access and staging at the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: How to provide media access while protecting operations and safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a media staging/briefing area that doesn't hinder operations, choose backgrounds carefully, assume reporters will record and don't tell them to stop, coordinate access to persons in charge, and use media pools when restricting access (allow representatives from TV, radio, print, internet). Do not choose pool members for them; let media decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8-Step communication model
rubrics_metrics.description: A structured social-marketing-based communications planning process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow steps: 1) Assess current situation (audience/problem/action); 2) Set communication goals and SMART objectives; 3) Identify intended audiences and segment/analyze them; 4) Develop and pretest messages (clear, concise, jargon-free, emphasize benefits); 5) Select channels and activities based on audience and partners; 6) Develop an action plan with backups and contingencies; 7) Develop and pretest materials (concept/positioning, memorability, readability, peer review, test marketing); 8) Implement, evaluate, and modify the plan as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretesting and evaluation of materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for testing communications materials before full deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct concept and positioning testing, assess memorability, impact, image, persuasiveness, and readability; consider peer/professional review; conduct limited test marketing with a sample of the target audience; plan metrics for measuring success and modify materials based on evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole community approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure communications and plans account for the entire community and partner resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know community demographics, governmental structure, key players, relevant history and culture. Design messages and outreach to serve diverse populations and leverage resources from government, NGOs, private sector, schools, healthcare, and other stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate vs. incident planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Different planning modes that affect PIO responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate planning occurs in non-emergency times and creates general procedures (e.g., NRF, state plans). Incident planning is specific to an impending or occurring incident (e.g., Incident Action Plan, strategic communications plan) and dovetails with the 8-step model and ICS incident planning processes.
